title: Deploying and validating a metropolitan QKD secure network: architecture and field performance
authors: Claudia De Lazzari, Nicola Biagi, Damiano Giani, Marco Russo, Fernando Chirici, Francesco Stocco, Saverio Francesconi, Giacomo Ferranti, Alessandro Soureal, Antonella Sanguineti, Bartolomeo Montrucchio, Christian Laurenzi, Oliviero Testa, Guglielmo Morgari, Antonio Manzalini, Tommaso Occhipinti, Alessandro Zavatta, Davide Bacco
abstract: The advent of cryptographically relevant quantum computers poses an existential threat to classical public-key infrastructure. Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) addresses this challenge by providing information-theoretic security for key establishment, independently of any computational hardness assumption. In this work, the deployment and experimental validation of a metropolitan-scale quantum-secure network between data centers in Milan is reported. The network operates over installed fiber infrastructure and implements a layered architecture integrating QKD hardware, standards-compliant Key Management (KM), and centralized Software-Defined Networking (SDN) orchestration. Dynamic path reconfiguration via active optical switching and trusted-node routing allow automated fail-over solutions. Application-layer validation across diverse protocols and workloads confirms the seamless interoperability of all system components. These results establish the technical and operational readiness of metropolitan QKD networks for production deployment, and offer a replicable blueprint for building quantum-secure communication infrastructure at metropolitan scale.
summary: This paper reports the experimental deployment and validation of a metropolitan Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) network across data centers in Milan. It proves that by integrating QKD hardware with layered key management and SDN orchestration, secure, information-theoretically protected communication can be achieved at scale. The results establish a replicable blueprint for quantum-secure infrastructure.
main_problem: The work addresses the existential threat posed by quantum computers to classical cryptography by deploying a Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) secure network.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated operational readiness for metropolitan-scale QKD networks, validating key establishment and service continuity across complex, reconfigurable topologies involving trusted nodes.
method: The validation involved testing the full system stack—from quantum key generation to application layer consumption—across multiple simulated link failures and path changes.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a metropolitan-scale QKD network connecting data centers in Milan, utilizing installed fiber infrastructure, layered architecture (QKD, KM, Encryption), and SDN orchestration.
key_observables: Secure Key Rate (SKR) stability, successful key propagation through trusted nodes, and sustained high-intensity throughput during application layer testing.
important_parameters: Metropolitan scale deployment, O-band (1310 nm) quantum transmission over installed dark fiber, and the use of standards-compliant Key Management (KM).
main_assumptions: The system operates in a realistic environment coexisting with production ICT systems, rather than a purely controlled lab setting.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the network architecture overview, SKR stability over time during link activation/switching, and color-coded active link intervals corresponding to different operational states.
paper_structure: The paper details the layered architecture (QKD $ightarrow$ KM $ightarrow$ Encryption), presents experimental validation across three test scenarios (direct, two-hop via trusted node, multi-hop), and concludes with application layer performance testing.
why_interesting: While focused on networking rather than fundamental physics, the work demonstrates practical quantum communication protocols and system integration challenges relevant to building large-scale quantum infrastructure.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Network architecture overview. The three red boxes represent the Points of Presence (PoPs): Milano Data4 (node D), Milano Caldera (node C), and Milano Malpaga. The latter PoP hosts two nodes — M1 and M2 — with the second implemented using a fiber spool for simulation purposes. The inset at the bottom right shows a high-level representation of the node configuration. Refer to the main text for a detailed description of the network.

Figure 2: Secure key rate (SKR) of the QKD network during the field trial. a) shows the performance of the point-to-point link between the Alice2 and Bob2 QKD devices, whereas b) refers to the switched links (Alice1M in node Malpaga M2, Alice1C in node Caldera, Alice1D in node Data4, and Bob1 in node Malpaga M1). In the latter plot, the height of each bar represents the mean SKR during the active period of the corresponding link, while its width reflects the time duration of the specific active configuration.
